notes.title: Propositions and truth values
notes.body: A proposition is a statement that is either true or false, never both. `p AND q` is true only when both are true; `p OR q` is true when at least one is true; `NOT p` flips the value. Worked example: evaluate `(p AND q) OR (NOT r)` at p=T, q=F, r=T. First `p AND q` = T AND F = F. Then `NOT r` = NOT T = F. Finally `F OR F` = **F**. So the whole expression is **F**. Work inside-out: parentheses first, then NOT, then AND, then OR — the same precedence habit that prevents bugs in code conditions.

notes.title: Truth tables, computed by enumeration
notes.body: A truth table lists every assignment of the variables. With n variables there are 2^n rows — for n=3 that is **8** rows, computed as 2^3. Worked example: the implication `p -> q`, defined as `(NOT p) OR q`. Its table: p=T,q=T -> T; p=T,q=F -> F; p=F,q=T -> T; p=F,q=F -> T. The only false row is true-premise/false-conclusion. Enumerating all rows mechanically (as the lab does in Python) removes all doubt: no case is forgotten, because the count 2^n proves the table is complete.

notes.title: De Morgan's laws, verified by brute force
notes.body: De Morgan's laws: `NOT (p AND q)` equals `(NOT p) OR (NOT q)`, and `NOT (p OR q)` equals `(NOT p) AND (NOT q)`. Worked verification: checking all 4 assignments of (p,q) in Python, every row agrees — **True**. This is the law behind simplifying negated conditions: `NOT (admin AND active)` becomes `NOT admin OR NOT active`. In code and in firewall/policy rules, pushing NOT inward with De Morgan turns an unreadable negated conjunction into a plain disjunction.

notes.title: Implication and the contrapositive
notes.body: `p -> q` (if p then q) is logically equivalent to its contrapositive `(NOT q) -> (NOT p)`. Worked verification: all 4 assignments agree — **True**. The converse `q -> p` is NOT equivalent (check p=T,q=F: implication false, converse true). Practical use: to prove 'if the build passes then tests ran', prove the contrapositive 'if tests did not run then the build fails' — often the easier direction. Confusing implication with converse is one of the most common logic errors in specifications.

notes.title: Predicate logic over finite domains
notes.body: Predicates add quantifiers: `FORALL x, P(x)` and `EXISTS x, P(x)`. Over a finite domain you can evaluate them by enumeration. Worked example: domain = {2, 3, 4}, statement `EXISTS x, x is prime AND x > 3`. Check: x=2 (prime, not >3, fails), x=3 (prime, not >3, fails), x=4 (not prime, fails). No witness exists, so the statement is **false**. Change `>3` to `>=3`: x=3 is prime and >= 3, so the statement becomes **true**. Existence claims need exactly one witness; universal claims need every case. This discipline maps directly onto testing: 'there exists an input that crashes' vs 'for all inputs it terminates'.

notes.title: Boolean algebra for systems work
notes.body: Boolean algebra gives simplification laws: absorption `p OR (p AND q) = p`, distribution, idempotence `p AND p = p`. Worked example: simplify `(admin AND active) OR (admin AND NOT active)`. Factor admin: `admin AND (active OR NOT active)` = `admin AND T` = **admin**. Verified by enumerating all 4 assignments of (admin, active): both sides agree on every row. Why it matters: access-policy engines evaluate exactly these expressions. Simplifying before deploying means fewer rules, faster evaluation, and policies a human can audit. Formal logic is the machinery for tiering claims without fooling yourself: valid argument forms keep DOCUMENTED separate from TRADITIONAL.

notes.title: Divisibility and primes
notes.body: d divides n if n = d·k for integer k. A prime has exactly two divisors. Worked example: factor 180. 180 = 2^2 × 3^2 × 5 (verify: 4×9×5 = 180). Primality testing by trial division only needs divisors up to √n: to test 97, check primes ≤ √97 ≈ 9.8, i.e. 2,3,5,7 — none divide, so 97 is prime. Unique prime factorization is the foundation everything below builds on.

notes.title: GCD and the Euclidean algorithm
notes.body: Worked example: gcd(48, 180). Euclid: 180 = 3×48 + 36; 48 = 1×36 + 12; 36 = 3×12 + 0. Last nonzero remainder: **12**. Python: math.gcd(48,180) = 12 — agreement. The extended algorithm also finds integers x,y with 48x+180y=gcd; those coefficients are exactly what the next note's inverse computation uses. GCD answers 'what's the largest shared structure' — from simplifying fractions to RSA key generation.

notes.title: Modular arithmetic
notes.body: a ≡ b (mod m) means m divides a−b. Worked examples mod 26: 17 + 10 = 27 ≡ 1; 17 × 3 = 51 ≡ 25; 100 mod 26 = **22** since 26×3=78 and 100−78=22. Addition, subtraction, multiplication all work mod m; division needs an inverse, which exists exactly when gcd(a,m)=1. Here gcd(17,26) = 1, so 17 has an inverse mod 26. Number theory also carries the historical thread of this course: number lore belongs to the TRADITIONAL tier unless primary sources say otherwise.

notes.title: Modular inverses, computed
notes.body: Worked example: inverse of 17 mod 26. Computed: 17^(-1) mod 26 = **23**. Verification: 17×23 = 391 = 26×15 + 1, so 17×23 ≡ **1** (mod 26) ✓. Solve 17x ≡ 5 (mod 26): multiply by the inverse, x ≡ 5×23 = 115 ≡ **11** (mod 26). Check: 17×11 = 187 ≡ 5 ✓. Inverses turn modular division into multiplication — the operation RSA decryption performs.

notes.title: Euler's totient
notes.body: φ(m) counts integers 1..m coprime to m. Worked example: φ(26). Counting k with gcd(k,26)=1 gives **12**. Euler's theorem: if gcd(a,m)=1 then a^φ(m) ≡ 1 (mod m). Check with a=3, m=26: φ=12, 3^12 mod 26 = **1** ✓. This theorem is why RSA decryption works: exponents reduce mod φ(n).

notes.title: Toy RSA, end to end
notes.body: Worked example with small primes p=61, q=53. n = 61×53 = **3233**; φ(n) = 60×52 = **3120**. Choose public exponent e=17 (coprime to φ). Private exponent d = e^(−1) mod φ = **2753**. Encrypt message 42: c = 42^17 mod 3233 = **2557**. Decrypt: m = 2557^2753 mod 3233 = **42** — the original message ✓. Every number here was computed, not asserted. Real RSA uses 2048-bit primes, but the mathematics is exactly this.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Corpus Hermeticum** — the dialogues attributed to Hermes Trismegistus; late-antique Alexandrian texts, not primeval Egyptian scripture.
- **Asclepius** — the most complete single Hermetic text; read it first.
- **Nag Hammadi** — the 1945 find that reframed the world the Hermetic texts belong to.
- **Late-antique Alexandria** — the syncretic city where Greek philosophy, Egyptian religion, and emerging Christianity met; the Corpus is what happens when they share a city.
- **Casaubon (1614)** — dated the Corpus to late antiquity by philology; the founding act of esoteric historiography. Texts have dates, and dates have consequences.
- **Cipher Manuscripts** — the Golden Dawn’s founding documents: DOCUMENTED as artifacts, CONTESTED as to origin; tier each claim separately.
- **Golden Dawn (1888–1903)** — the order of Westcott, Mathers, and Woodman, through the schisms; read its grade papers as a curriculum, not a mystery.
- **Grade system** — the ladder from 0=0 upward; a syllabus: what’s taught, in what order, to what end.
- **LBRP** — the Lesser Banishing Ritual of the Pentagram; a Golden Dawn paper and our study object. Note what the papers say vs. what later books claim.
- **Gardnerian Wicca** — Wicca’s documented origins; tier the origin claims as you meet them.
- **Thelema** — Crowley’s current: A.’.’A.’., O.T.O., and the Book of the Law.
- **Book of the Law** — primary text first, Crowley’s commentaries second, others’ opinions last.
- **Sigilization** — Austin Osman Spare’s technique: DOCUMENTED as technique, CONTESTED as mechanism.
- **Paradigm shifting** — Peter Carroll’s chaos-magical move: belief as instrument, a tool rather than a truth-claim.
- **Principia Discordia** — the Discordian scripture; chaos magic’s irreverent cousin.
- **Tree of Life** — the Hermetic Qabalah’s map; a memory palace organizing planets, elements, and tarot, whatever else it is.
- **Correspondences** — the Qabalistic system of linkages across planets, elements, and tarot.
- **Paracelsus** — iatrochemistry: alchemy as early chemistry and medicine; “the dose makes the poison” is alchemy’s most DOCUMENTED contribution to science.
- **DOCUMENTED** — primary sources, artifacts, dated texts: the bedrock tier.
- **SCHOLARLY CONSENSUS** — what historians agree on: provisional, cited.
- **TRADITIONAL** — what lineages claim about themselves: reported, not endorsed.
- **CONTESTED** — open questions and rival readings: where the seminar lives.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Before we theorize, we practice the one reflex this academy exists to build: tiering a claim. You’ll use the Tiering Engine lab (il01-lab-tier) — but the procedure is identical on paper.

1. **Choose one claim** from this module’s readings — for example, “The Corpus Hermeticum preserves primeval Egyptian wisdom.”
2. **Split it into atomic sub-claims:** (a) the manuscripts exist and date to late antiquity; (b) their content originates in primeval Egypt.
3. **Collect the evidence you actually hold** for each sub-claim: the manuscript tradition and Casaubon’s 1614 philology for (a); lineage assertion for (b).
4. **Run each sub-claim** through the lab’s tier_claim function with its evidence string, and read the (tier, justification) pairs it returns.
5. **Record every pair in your tiered reading journal** with the evidence cited — the justification matters more than the label.
6. **Circle the CONTESTED sub-claims.** Those are not failures; they are your seminar questions for the rest of the academy.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body:
The brief. Choose one text from this module — the Asclepius, a Golden Dawn grade paper, or a passage of the Book of the Law — and produce a tiered dossier a historian would respect.

Deliverables. (1) A claim inventory: every factual claim the text or its surrounding tradition makes about origins, authorship, and transmission. (2) A tier for each claim — DOCUMENTED, SCHOLARLY CONSENSUS, TRADITIONAL, or CONTESTED — with the evidence cited. (3) One CONTESTED question argued both ways, about 300 words per side. notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Esoteric material punishes sloppy epistemics harder than most subjects. These are the failure modes that separate scholars from storytellers in Hermetic Foundations:
- **Collapsing the tiers.** The single most common failure: treating a TRADITIONAL claim as DOCUMENTED because it feels old. Every claim you touch in Hermetic Foundations gets an explicit tier — DOCUMENTED, SCHOLARLY CONSENSUS, TRADITIONAL, or CONTESTED — before you use it.

- **Single-source trust.** One grimoire, one translation, one blogger is not a consensus. Corroborate across at least two independent sources before a claim leaves your notes.
- **Belief creep.** Studying a system is not joining it. Keep the scholar's bracket: you can map a cosmology precisely while suspending assent. Losing the bracket turns analysis into apologetics.
- **Etymology as evidence.** Word origins are interesting and prove almost nothing about historical claims. 'The word X comes from Y' is a linguistic fact, not a historical argument about Hermetic Foundations.
- **Skipping the primary source.** Summaries of summaries drift. Read the actual passage — even in translation — before you argue about what a Hermetic Foundations text says.

(3) A verdict of about 500 words argued both ways: the strongest case that the circuit is real, and the strongest case that it is mystified feedback. (4) The Cybersyn contrast: one page on what honest tiering looks like when applied to a documented build versus its mythology.

The standard. The theory’s CONTESTED status is not a defect to hide — it is the seminar’s subject. You are graded on whether your tiers hold and your evidence is dated, never on which side you take.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Hyperstition is presented as a CONTESTED theory throughout — the seminar’s job is to map the argument, not to settle it. Land’s post-1990s work is a separate question and out of scope; we read the 1990s corpus. Cybersyn’s documented build (telex network, VSM design, ops room, 1971–73) and its mythologized legacy are different tiers, and we never let the legend borrow the build’s credibility. Meme chaos-magic is taught as hypothesis — the chaos-magic lineage is real, the network-age extension is argued, not asserted. Original study material; no credential conferred; assessments test whether you can map the circuit and tier the claims — never what you believe.

notes.title: Worked example: Hyperstitional circuit?
notes.body:
**Problem.** Hyperstitional circuit?

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** belief→action→reality→belief
- **Why:** The feedback loop — ideas bootstrapping themselves into reality. (Concepts: hyperstitional circuit.)

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *The feedback loop — ideas bootstrapping themselves into reality.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Esoteric material punishes sloppy epistemics harder than most subjects. These are the failure modes that separate scholars from storytellers in The CCRU Seminar: Hyperstition and Cybernetics:
- **Collapsing the tiers.** The single most common failure: treating a TRADITIONAL claim as DOCUMENTED because it feels old. Every claim you touch in The CCRU Seminar: Hyperstition and Cybernetics gets an explicit tier — DOCUMENTED, SCHOLARLY CONSENSUS, TRADITIONAL, or CONTESTED — before you use it.
- **Anachronism.** Reading modern meanings back into period terms. When a The CCRU Seminar: Hyperstition and Cybernetics source says 'spirit', 'energy', or 'science', find what the word meant to the author, not what it means on social media.
- **Single-source trust.** One grimoire, one translation, one blogger is not a consensus. Corroborate across at least two independent sources before a claim leaves your notes.
- **Belief creep.** Studying a system is not joining it. Keep the scholar's bracket: you can map a cosmology precisely while suspending assent. Losing the bracket turns analysis into apologetics.
- **Etymology as evidence.** Word origins are interesting and prove almost nothing about historical claims. 'The word X comes from Y' is a linguistic fact, not a historical argument about The CCRU Seminar: Hyperstition and Cybernetics.
- **Skipping the primary source.** Summaries of summaries drift. Read the actual passage — even in translation — before you argue about what a The CCRU Seminar: Hyperstition and Cybernetics text says.

scriptLabs.title: The Tiering Engine
scriptLabs.brief: Build a claim-tiering function: given a claim about an esoteric text, classify it DOCUMENTED / SCHOLARLY CONSENSUS / TRADITIONAL / CONTESTED with a justification. The method as code.
scriptLabs.starter:
def tier_claim(claim, evidence):
    # YOUR TASK: return (tier, justification)
    # DOCUMENTED: primary source / artifact / date
    # SCHOLARLY CONSENSUS: historians agree (cite)
    # TRADITIONAL: lineage claims it
    # CONTESTED: open debate
    pass

tests = [
    ('The Corpus Hermeticum manuscripts date to late antiquity', 'Casaubon 1614 philology; manuscript tradition'),
    ('The Golden Dawn was founded by ancient adepts', 'lineage origin story; Cipher MS debate'),
    ('Dee kept angel diaries 1581-1589', 'the diaries exist in archives'),
]
for claim, ev in tests:
    print(tier_claim(claim, ev))
scriptLabs.hint: Keyword routing: 'manuscript/archive/exists' → DOCUMENTED; 'lineage claims/origin story' → TRADITIONAL (or CONTESTED if debated); 'historians agree' → SCHOLARLY CONSENSUS.

answerBank.q: Do I have to believe any of this?
answerBank.a: No — assessments test literacy, never belief. The tier system exists precisely so you can study claims rigorously without affirming them. Read, tier, argue.

answerBank.q: Why study esotericism in a tech academy?
answerBank.a: Historiography, primary-source literacy, and the tier discipline transfer everywhere — including to evaluating technical claims. Plus: the history of computing (Dee, cybernetics) runs through this material.

answerBank.q: Isn't the CCRU just internet mysticism?
answerBank.a: The seminar treats it as texts with a documented context (Warwick, 1990s) and a CONTESTED theory (hyperstition). Read the corpus, tier the claims, argue the status — that's the work.
The Asclepius (complete, short), then Dee's biography, then the Land/CCRU corpus in reading order. Commonplace book from day one.

answerBank.q: How do TRADITIONAL claims get treated?
